lesson.title: The Physics of Cooling Coffee
lesson.summary: Newton's law of cooling says an object's temperature changes fastest when it is far from its surroundings and levels off as it approaches room temperature, and the derivative makes that precise.
lesson.body:
Newton's law of cooling states that an object's temperature changes at a rate proportional to the difference between its own temperature and the ambient temperature around it: T'(t) = -k * (T(t) - T_ambient), for some positive constant k. Solving that relationship gives the exponential model T(t) = T_ambient + (T0 - T_ambient) * e^(-k t), where T0 is the starting temperature. The intuition matches everyday experience: a cup of hot coffee loses heat quickly at first, when it is much hotter than the room, and cools more and more slowly as its temperature approaches room temperature.

Consider coffee cooling in a room held at 20 degrees Celsius, following T(t) = 20 + 60 * e^(-0.1 t), with t in minutes. At t = 0, T(0) = 20 + 60 = 80 degrees Celsius, a reasonable starting temperature for a freshly poured cup. Differentiating gives T'(t) = 60 * (-0.1) * e^(-0.1 t) = -6 * e^(-0.1 t) degrees Celsius per minute.

At t = 0, T'(0) = -6 degrees Celsius per minute: the coffee is losing heat quickly right after pouring, and the negative sign confirms the temperature is decreasing, exactly as rate interpretation says it should. Ten minutes later, T(10) = 20 + 60 * e^(-1), which is approximately 42.07 degrees Celsius, and T'(10) = -6 * e^(-1), approximately -2.21 degrees Celsius per minute. The coffee has cooled substantially and is now losing heat much more slowly than it did at the start.

That slowdown is exactly Newton's law at work, and it is easy to check directly: -0.1 * (T(10) - 20) = -0.1 * 22.07, which is approximately -2.21, matching T'(10) computed straight from the derivative. The math here is structurally the same exponential decay seen in population rate, just with the sign of the exponent flipped and the proportionality tied to the distance from an ambient temperature rather than to the quantity itself. As always, the sign of the derivative tells the direction (cooling, since it is negative) and its size tells the speed, in degrees Celsius per minute, which is exactly the rate interpretation habit built earlier in this chapter sequence.
